source: Never forget that I'm here.
And Ophelia's here, even if she likes to skulk around pretending we don't see her.
And as long as you have friends in this world, you can do just about anything.
Now go about your business as usual. But keep your head turned up and your shoulders back. Act like the King you will be.
Indeed. Indeed, I will.
Thank you both. This was... this is... exactly what I needed.
You know where to find me if you need me.
If there were... someone who could show me how, give me advice...
Ophelia. The time has come for me to make a decision.
How have your first days as Prince-Elect gone?
Quickly. Frighteningly.
I'm not ready to be King.
Perhaps no one is, really.
My uncle was. He committed a grave sin to achieve it.
But in the end, he was no more fit than any other man.
He reached for the crown, but could not keep it. Denmark has struggled under his rule, I'm told.
The situation is worse than I thought. We have to fix things, Ophelia. It's going to be a long path forward.
All that assuming the nobility will elect me to the position, of course.
You know... I realized something today.
As I contemplated all these decisions before me, I thought to myself—what would Ophelia say of this?
I need you by my side if we're to bring great things to this country.
Without you, I'm... nothing.
Hamlet, I've even less experience than you do at managing affairs of state.
Yes—but you understand people. The way they think. What they love and fear most.
And you understand how to fix people, too. You understand that healing is more powerful than destroying.
That's something Claudius never understood. He saw power and reached for it without understanding that power obtained through fear is fragile.
Then let's establish a new way.
Tell me. What have you decided? How will you rule?
Rosie and Guilda... told I ought to think of myself.
They want to return to Wittenberg, and for me to join them.
Wittenberg? At a time like this?
I must admit, I found something tempting in the notion.
Many Prince-Elects have gone abroad in a time of mourning. It would only be a short stay.
That's foolish. You know how foolish that would be. How can you even consider it?
You're right. Of course you're right.
Forget I even raised the subject. It was just a fleeting notion.
My first matter of concern was to understand where the biggest threat to the throne of Denmark lies.
I know that the Danish nobility are deeply unhappy at the present moment.
As Claudius largely ignored them, their fealty trended towards Norway's growing power. Now they're borderline treasonous.
As much as I would have liked to receive some advice here, I heard none.
So I shall move forward under my original instinct.
Most people who came to speak with me offered me the advice to be forceful with the nobility.
My father would have handled this matter by riding out in full decorum to greet these men, reminding them of their King's presence.
I intend to do the same. Perhaps once the noblemen see me in person, they shall remember that I am my father's son, not Claudius's.
However, the advice I received surprised me. It became clear to me that the biggest threat is truly within my own court.
I now believe the nobility can wait. My first order of business will be to provide clarity and peace here. That peace shall come soon.
The second matter of concern is, predictably, understanding who will rule beside me.
When the world thought me just a mad Prince it wasn't a popular topic, but once you inherit a crown, everyone looks at you like you're a piece of meat.
For better or worse, my betrothal to Brit was timely.
As Prince, I could marry for love. As King, I must wield marriage as a tool. The marriage I make can improve the world or leave things as they are.
She'll unite her family's power with mine. Things will be stable, if dreadfully dull.
Try to sound a mite more excited on your wedding day, at least.
When I thought about becoming King, I knew I'd have to learn to put aside the idle dreams I had before.
But I always believed I'd marry for love. Putting that dream aside will be the hardest of all.
Though Brit and I won't be married now, of course, it changed the way I thought about this process.
My wife will likely be another powerful family's daughter.
In short, I must make a proposal.
Being with you again has made me happier than I ever thought possible in a time like this.
But something changed, Ophelia.
When you asked my mother to speak with me, she was honest with me. So honest, it sent me reeling.
My mother's advice was that my life is no longer my own. It belongs to my country. And I must use my life in service to improving my countrymen's.
So as much as it goes against everything I've ever wanted, I'm choosing to follow Mother's advice.
I'm going to marry Brit, uniting her powerful family with our house.
Brit was the obvious candidate. But... no longer.
My wife will likely be another Brockenhuus, or perhaps another powerful family's daughter.
(Hmm. I ought to have known Gertrude would give him that sort of advice.)
Do what you must. I am only sorry that our dalliance made your decision all the harder.
Never say that. If I could choose my own fate-- it's always been you, Ophelia. You know that.
I must admit I found myself dwelling on what I'd say to you now.
But now that we're here, the speech is failing me.
Hmm. I have an idea.
It's a lovely night for a walk, don't you think?
Would you accompany me?
Of course we'd end up here.
Is something wrong? We can go elsewhere, if you like.
No—this is fine. But Hamlet, what is it about this graveyard you find so compelling?
I feel as though you've been lurking here for years. You're a permanent fixture at this point.
Truth be told, I cannot say, precisely.
Perhaps it's the solitude. The emptiness. I can rest assured no one will bother me here.
Or—maybe it's the certainty of death in an otherwise-uncertain world. There's something comforting in that.
Hm. Morbid.
I prefer 'practical'.
And besides, haven't you often wondered what it must be like to die?
To die, to sleep, perchance to dream..
No. I don't have to wonder. I've already died. There is no dream. There is nothing at all.
Or perhaps this is the dream, forever repeating itself—a fever dream, more like.
Yes. Perhaps this is what death is truly like, for all. And you and I are simply illusions. Ghosts.
You're worrying me.
Don't mind me.
Hamlet. Earlier you mentioned you'd wanted me for some time.
How do you know it's not merely familiarity?
How do you know this is more than the happenstance closeness we've experienced for so long?
Even when we were lovers, I often thought—soon you'll grow bored, or exhausted, or irritated of me at some point.
My father often warned me you would.
I wasn't sure before, myself.
I didn't know until recently, in fact.
When I was at Wittenberg I was surrounded by men and women in the midst of a great rebirth. Arts, culture, knowledge—it was fantastic.
The world is changing around us. The future is thrilling. New ways of governing and thinking and building, all possible and within my grasp.
I attended every gala and low-brow party I was invited to. I danced and I drank and I wandered with abandon. And—
I was with other women.
I assumed you were. You don't need to flush red like that.
It's embarrassing to admit that to you. Because, of course, the only thing I learned was that all other women were nothing like you.
But—I knew—or I thought—things had ended between us, that you would never want me near you once more.
And so I tried to forge new connections, find new faces to dream about. And some of them made my heart throb weakly, but none with as much passion as you.
All I could think about, whenever I saw some new marvel or heard some magnificent lecture, was—'I wish she could hear this.'
'I wonder what she would think.'
Ophelia, you are everything to me. And I'm going to spend the rest of my life showing you how true that is.
Now you're making me flush.
There's something I need to say.
I want to ask for your hand in marriage.
What? Really? Now?
Quite a sudden change of heart from only a week ago, don't you think?
You know me. You know I'm quite serious.
I don't doubt you are.
What would this mean for your—my—future?
We'll uncover that much together.
For now, all that matters is that you're the one helping me make these decisions.
There's no one else whose mind I trust more implicitly, no one I've known half so deeply.
...And something else has weighed heavily upon me.
You recall that altercation on the boat, with Lady Guildenstern.
When I was on board our ship to England... Lady Guildenstern took me aside.
I cannot promise that the world will always be kind to you if you stand at my side.
I understand there are forces at work beyond both of our control. The world is a hateful place.
But I have to believe there's a way we can work to root out that vileness wherever it lives.
Both in the world, and in me.
My time on the throne will be markedly different from the men before me. There will be no more calls for blood or shows of force.
The era for that has passed.
Will you become the future Queen of Denmark?
Agree to marry Hamlet?

source: I cannot deny you would have been my first choice. But in all these days, you've said not a thing.
I will.
Oh... ha. My heart's fluttering as fast as a rat's. I can hardly breathe.
Your face is so pale. You look absolutely frightened.
You do terrify me thoroughly. Er, I mean that in the nicest possible way.
No offense taken.
And I wasn't sure you would say yes.
Neither was I, truly. But I want to see where this path leads with you.
I think you'll make a wonderful king, in time.
I don't think I can properly convey how much I've missed you.
Even as I'm terrified I'll hurt you.
Then don't hurt me. It's not complicated.
Heh. When did you get so bold?
I've changed. My life has been strange lately. Let's leave it at that.
I... I can't remember the last time I felt this happy.
All that's left is to tell the others.
